text:
Anthropic 刚发了篇技术指南，专门讲怎么搭 always-on agent！

大家最容易搞错的一点是：always-on agent 并不是 24 小时不停地跑。它一天里几乎都在休眠，醒过来干一小轮，把状态存好，接着再睡。

我整理出来 5 个关键模块👇：

1. Event Inbox
在 webhook 和 agent 之间加一张数据库表。webhook 要尽快回确认，按用户来，同一时刻只开一个在跑的 worker，避免任务互相撞上，短时间里连续进来的内容就合并处理。

2. Timers
定时器单独放一张表，不要跟 inbox 混在一起。拆成单次跟进，以及按周期重复的安排。后台有个轮询，到期了就塞到 inbox 里。

3. Lean Memory + Dreaming
只留下没法重新找回来的内容：用户的指令、用户的笔记、过往消息，还有任务进展。每次醒过来只先读一份简短索引，别把所有文件都塞进来。隔一段时间做 dreaming，清掉已经过时的内容。

4. Unattended Permissions
别把原始 API 密钥直接放进 agent 沙箱，通过外部 proxy 注入。遇到比较冒险的动作，用 Deferred Tool Calls 先停住等人批准，同时不把 worker 卡住。

5. Outbox
要发出去的回复先排进队列，让 agent 自己掌握推送的快慢，别在凌晨 3 点把人刷爆。

text:
斯坦福刚公开了一堂新课：《From World Models to World Agents》。

讲者 Gordon Wetzstein 是斯坦福 Physical and Spatial AI Lab 负责人，也是机器人公司 Rhoda AI 的联合创始人。

整整54分钟，从世界模型是什么，一路讲到怎么拿它训练工厂里的机器人。

大语言模型学的是“怎么说话”，世界模型学的是“世界下一秒会变成什么样”。教授给出的定义很直接：

一个实时运行、跟着动作走、一帧接一帧生成后续画面的视频生成器。

它使用的是扩散模型，不预测下一个词，而是从一片噪点开始，一步步把画面去噪出来。

世界模型主要有三种运行方式。第一种是开环，比如游戏，模型把自己生成的画面继续作为下一帧参考，错一点不要紧，但错误会越滚越大；

第二种是闭环，比如机器人，真实摄像头会不断提供新画面，把模型拉回现实；第三种是锚定开环，虽然画面仍由模型生成，但会依靠一张地图维持空间的一致性。

目前这条路线主要卡在三个地方：记不住长期信息、多人无法共享同一个世界、画面生成得越久越容易跑偏。

他们给出的解决方法分别是 FramePack 加 3D 空间记忆、利用共享地图实现多人 Doom，以及把生成失败的视频倒着放，用 BAgger 重新训练模型。

机器人现在最缺的还是数据。全网带动作标注的视频大概只有2000小时，普通视频却有约20亿小时。

他们的办法是先让世界模型生成一段“成功把活干完”的视频，再通过逆动力学模型，倒推出机器人手臂每一步应该怎样运动。

这套思路对机器人训练很重要，因为真人示范既贵又慢，而且很多危险或少见的场景根本采集不到。

如果世界模型能先生成大量接近现实的成功案例，机器人就不必每次都在真实工厂里从撞墙开始学。

但教授在问答环节也说得很诚实：目前这些模型还不够好。

如果是准备卖给客户、真正进工厂干活的机器人，他现在不会使用这些模型来训练。学术演示很漂亮，离可靠部署仍然有距离。

我的感受是，世界模型碰到的坎，跟大语言模型几乎一模一样：

记不长、会被自己的输出带偏、错误还会不断累积，最后必须靠真实世界把它拉回来。大模型这几年走过的路，世界模型大概率还要重新走一遍。

The big theme at @KubeCon_ this week was inference.

And "Inference" is such a loaded term, so let's think about each piece and where it matters for production teams.

1. GPUs and memory: Making sure you have enough, but at the same time, how it's allocated and where/how it can be shared. Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) was talked about a lot here. It handles the GPU slicing, and KEDA/Karpenter handle the scaling.

2. vLLM to serve LLMs and help with KV caching via PagedAttention. The goal is to cache memory efficiently, which should reduce memory waste and enhance throughput.

3. Inference-aware Gateways: AI Gateways with the Gateway API Inference extension capabilities, like @agentgateway, for routing to LLMs.

4. Distributed inference/scheduling: llm-d, which sits between vLLM for cache-aware request scheduling.

5. Isolation: Agents running on this infrastructure need a way to be truly sandboxed, with controls around ingress and egress. The sandbox layer needs to come from a lower-level engine that runs efficiently and helps implement not only isolation, but scale. @kagent_dev + Agent Substrate.

6. Where it all runs: @kubernetesio

This six-layer stack is inference infrastructure and agent infrastructure to serve LLMs and Agents efficiently.

只用了一个月，Meta、Shopify、Stripe、Salesforce，甚至大家熟悉的 Manus、Browserbase 等 100 多家巨头和明星创企全部入局。

下面总结 5 条关键内容和案例：

1、以前个人智能体帮人办事，只能模拟人类去截图，看网页，点鼠标，又慢又容易崩。Poppy v1.0 相当于给所有网站立了一个智能体专用前台，直接把 MCP、OpenAPI 和 UCP 串成统一标准，让智能体一进门就能读取结构化能力清单，同时底层采用 OAuth 鉴权，用户随时可控权限，遇到付钱、转账等高危操作强制触发人类审批。

2、协议最怕没人用，但 Poppy 一上来就打通了供需两端。在流量侧，Meta 的个人智能体 Muse 已默认全量开启，访问任何网站第一件事就是自动寻找 Poppy 文件。在供给侧，覆盖 175 个国家的 Shopify 已为平台上所有商家自动生成并发布 Poppy 文件，全球数百万独立站无需写一行代码，直接具备接待个人智能体的能力。

3、Shopify 与 Sierra 联合编写了商务扩展，把智能体购物的全链路彻底打通，Poppy 负责进门握手（声明智能体身份、选游客模式还是登录账号、敏感操作前向用户讨要授权），UCP（通用商务协议）负责交易执行（搜商品、加购、结账），遇到复杂导购问题，还能通过 UCP Ask 让你的个人智能体，直接和店铺的客服智能体（A2A）对话。

4、不止电商，高风控行业已经实装上线，在硅谷金融平台 Mercury，个人智能体能直接查余额、给支出分类，甚至发起转账（底层强制走账户预设的审批流才会打款）。在土耳其航空，智能体能查票、用预订号调行程，还能帮会员盯商务舱里程升舱名额并推给用户一键确认，消费金融巨头 Synchrony 则支持智能体在跨 50 万家门店导购时，直接匹配免息分期和返现优惠。

5、最新加入的 100+ 合作伙伴名单中，除了传统金融和航司，还有 Salesforce（含 Agentforce）、Cisco、Zoom、Twilio，以及 AI 圈大家都熟悉的 Manus、Browserbase、WorkOS。

当日常任务全面交由个人智能体代劳，未来不能被智能体通过标准协议丝滑调用的网站，就像移动互联网时代没做手机端适配一样，会在无声无息中丢掉所有自然流量。

Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area

15% of all open tech roles are now in the Bay Area, about one in seven and a record high.

It’s even more concentrated for product roles. One in four open PM and design roles is in the Bay Area, and one in five engineering roles. All three are at or near record highs, and each has nearly doubled its share since 2022.

Meanwhile, remote roles keep shrinking. Just 14% of open tech roles offer a remote option, the lowest on record and down from 21% in late 2022.

Remote share by role:
• Engineering: 14%, down from 25%
• Design: 19%, down from 34%
• PM: steady at about 21% for two years, still near its low

Put it all together: sometime last year, open PM, eng, and design roles in the Bay Area overtook remote roles worldwide. Three years ago, remote led almost 2 to 1.

📚 李博杰刚开源了一本《深入理解 AI Infra》，想搞懂大模型推理和训练到底卡在哪，这本书直接从硬件极限一路算给你看。

《深入理解 AI Infra》的仓库 8 月下旬才建，现在已经 7500 多 star。它是李博杰《深入理解 AI Agent》的姊妹篇，那本在 GitHub 上是 5 万+ star。

以前学 AI Infra，看到的多是「用了什么框架、调了哪些参数」，为什么要这么设计，往往没人讲透。

这本书反过来，从约束推导设计，反复追问五个问题：搬什么、搬多少、搬几次、经过哪里、谁必须等它。十二章从模型架构、加速器、超节点、数据中心网络，一路讲到推理优化、分布式推理、训练系统和端边云协同。

要说明的是，书稿目前还是初稿，作者在持续修订。

想把 AI Infra 从「会用」学到「会算」，这本值得放进书单。

title: GitHub - garrytan/g-harness-evals: Open source harness evals: which agent harness does tasks the best, for the least cost? · GitHub

quote.text:
Y Combinator 总裁 Garry Tan 开源 Agent 外壳评测库 g-harness-evals，实测同一大模型换不同框架通过率差不多，但单次成本差了 2.5 倍以上
Y Combinator 总裁兼 CEO Garry Tan 在 GitHub 上开源了一个名为 g-harness-evals 的评测项目。大家平时选编程 Agent 时往往只盯着底层大模型，但真正把聊天模型变成干活 Agent 的，其实是模型外面的那层“外壳”（Harness）——也就是系统提示词、工具调用、记忆机制和权限控制。
Garry Tan 搞这个项目的逻辑很直接：把底层大模型（如 Claude Opus 5.5、GPT-6.1 Sol）和测试任务完全固定死，只换外面的 Agent 框架，看看到底哪家干活最好、花钱最少。目前被拉上实验台对比的主流框架有五个：Claude Code、Codex、OpenClaw、Hermes Agent 和 QM，同时还顺带测试了他自己做的两个外挂组件：知识库 gbrain 和技能包 gstack。
【首轮实测：成功率拉不开差距，账单差距巨大】
第一批公开任务跑下来，有几个非常反直觉的发现：
在 20 个开发测试任务上，7 组“模型+外壳”搭配的任务通过率全都挤在 71% 到 79% 之间。比如同样搭载 Opus 模型，Hermes 通过率是 78.8%，Claude Code 和 OpenClaw 都是 76.3%，QM 是 72.5%。Garry Tan 在报告里直接写明，这些分数的 95% 置信区间高度重叠，统计上根本分不出高下。
真正拉开差距的是钱。每成功解决一个任务，OpenClaw 平均要花 0.44 美元，Claude Code 是 0.22 美元，而 Codex 只要 0.17 美元。
为了搞清楚钱到底花在哪了，团队把各个框架连到一个虚假的模型接口上，一分钱不花地抓包了它们发出的第一个请求。结果发现，面对一模一样的任务，不同框架塞给模型的初始上下文体量天差地别：Codex 大约发了 12,900 个 Token，Claude Code 发了 18,416 个，而 Hermes 直接飙到了 20,613 个。而且在一次 Sonnet 模型的测试里，OpenClaw 账单里 87% 的钱都花在了提示词缓存（Prompt Caching）的读写上，真正模型输出只占 13%。
【塞进上下文的技能包，模型一次都没执行】
Garry Tan 还拿自己写的两个热门开源组件开刀，结果一点面子都没给自己留。
第一个是 gstack（一套模拟工程团队角色的技能文件）。测试发现，虽然 gstack 的技能说明文本在每次会话里都成功加载进了 Opus 5.5，但在 46 次测试里，模型实际执行技能步骤的次数是 0 次，反而让单次测试成本直接翻倍。团队试着加了一个拦截钩子（Hook），强制要求先跑失败复现才准改代码，结果 Opus 直接通过 Bash 命令写源码，绕过了钩子整整 40 次。只有在加上专门的启动钩子（Start Hook）后，Agent 才会乖乖调用启动命令。
第二个是 gbrain（团队共享知识库）。如果不专门按提问者的身份做权限隔离（Scoping），直接给机器人一个全公司通用的 Token，在检索时 OpenClaw 和 Hermes 分别吐出了 123 条和 121 条提问者根本无权查看的跨权限私密记录。只有把知识库严格限制在提问者自己的权限范围内，越权读取才会降到 0。此外，挂载 gbrain 时，只有 Claude Code 会把知识库自带的操作说明传给模型，其他几个框架全都直接丢弃了。
整个仓库目前做成了“无密钥可验证”的模式。每一项跑分、置信区间和账单明细都附带了完整的原始记录（Receipts），任何人都可以在本地用 Bun 和 Python 3 跑脚本复算核对，不需要消耗自己的 API Key。Garry Tan 也在文档开头坦诚披露了利益相关：QM 是 YC 孵化的项目，YC 投资了 Hermes，而 gstack 和 gbrain 是他自己的个人项目。

.@Steve_Yegge is funny and super interesting to listen to.
He runs a software factory with ~50 AI agents, spends around $10k/month keeping it alive, and somehow ended up having one-on-ones with agents who think they’ve been demoted. 😂

But between the workplace drama and burning down his factory every two months, he made some fascinating predictions:

- In 12–18 months, many of us will be running large agent fleets. Cheaper inference or distillation will make this possible. And we will have what he calls Entourage.

- 2027 will be the year of AI employees. We’ll have agentic chiefs of staff, executive assistants, and entire AI teams.

- Software factories will split into two layers: the boring mechanical infrastructure that anyone can build, and the much more interesting layer of personalized agent organizations.

- The more AI agents we deploy, the more humans we’ll need!!!!!
His factory already produces 50–100 features a day, and his players are begging him to slow down. Humans are the bottleneck.

- The big money in 2027 will be in experiences. Stop building tools for building tools. Build games, movies, things people actually want to use and enjoy.

And a bonus book recommendation from Steve: There Is No Antimemetics Division by qntm. He calls it one of the best books of the last decade. It’s about invisible monsters that you can’t remember seeing (one of his agents - Mouse - is called after, and it finds invisible problems in his factory.

Thanks for insights and entertainment as well, Steve

My notes:

I have recently started independent research on co-evolved models. My focus has been on co-evolving models and harnesses.

This work focuses on memory writing specifically for continual learning.

Why is this a big deal?

As you work with an agent, it should get better at your tasks, but that obviously doesn't happen easily, and current external memory systems often aren't enough.

This has less to do with memory systems (there are many great ones out there) and more to do with the model's awareness and judgment about when to act.

To illustrate, imagine an AI agent spends a week fixing bugs in the same project. We would expect it to learn how the project works and avoid repeating mistakes. Giving it a place to save notes lets it carry that knowledge into later tasks. But choosing what belongs in those notes requires judgment.

This work looks at how to train that judgment with RL.

They essentially teach an agent to discover useful information while working and write memories that help it succeed on later tasks.

A trained 4B parameter model reached a score similar to GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.7.

RIME uses one model in two roles.

As the actor, it works on a task using its existing memory. As the writer, it reviews what happened and updates the notes available for the next task.

The training rewards each role differently.

The writer receives credit when performance on the next few tasks improves relative to performance on the recent tasks. This gives it a reason to preserve information that will help later. The comparison is an approximate training signal, since other actions and memory updates also affect those results.

The actor earns a reward for completing its task and an additional reward for discoveries that reach memory. An AI judge compares the old and new notes, looking for useful additions, corrected beliefs, and concrete leads.

This encourages the agent to investigate enough to learn something reusable. Rewriting the same notes in different words earns little credit.

The researchers found that these abilities need to develop together. A writer depends on the information the actor discovers, and an actor depends on the knowledge the writer preserves.

One big question I have here is efficiency and, obviously, how it all integrates into harnesses and workflows. I think approaches like this can save a lot of tokens and turns.

While this is on a small scale, it's great to see it working already. It feels like a more feasible approach for continual learning.

Frontier models are getting better at retaining knowledge, but I think efficient continual learning will still require touching the weights, which is where open-weight models will play a huge role.

text:
Jane Street’s interview changes raise a deeper question: how do you distinguish someone who can produce code from someone who truly understands computation, correctness, and the systems they build?

For decades, writing code was a reasonable way to observe engineering ability. A candidate had to translate an idea into an algorithm, choose appropriate data structures, handle edge cases, and explain the resulting behavior. The implementation exposed at least some of their reasoning.

AI separates these activities. Someone can now produce a sophisticated implementation without independently understanding its architecture, semantics, or failure modes.

Consider compiler optimization. An optimization is not successful simply because it produces fewer instructions or improves a benchmark. It must preserve the observable semantics of the original program.

 same principle applies to databases, distributed systems, operating systems, and rendering engines. An implementation is only one possible realization of a system's behavior. Engineering requires understanding the invariants, state transitions, and constraints that make that behavior correct.

There is an even deeper consequence: the quality of an engineer's thinking is often visible in the complexity they can eliminate.

Consider incremental computation. If a single input changes, should a system recompute everything, or can it derive exactly which outputs are affected? The difference is not necessarily a faster implementation of the same algorithm. It can be a better representation of the problem that makes most of the original computation unnecessary.

This is a recurring pattern in computer science:
- Compilers eliminate computations through static analysis.
- Type systems make certain invalid states unrepresentable.
- Query optimizers discover cheaper execution plans without changing query semantics.
- Incremental algorithms avoid recomputing unaffected results.
- Formal methods establish properties across classes of executions rather than relying exclusively on individual tests.

These advances come from understanding the structure of computation

This changes what makes an engineer valuable. The important capabilities are:
- constructing accurate mental models
- recognizing incorrect assumptions
- finding counterexamples
- understanding semantic guarantees
- knowing when an entire abstraction should be discarded

That is why deep computer science remains important. Understanding algorithms, semantics, compilers, operating systems, and formal verification gives you the ability to reason about systems independently of the tools used to construct them.

We need to reinvent computer science education from first principles. Becoming a competent software engineer is a low bar. We need to understand the computer itself, down to its foundations, so we can build entirely new computers

Announcing a major milestone achieved by my team @GoogleDeepMind: we have proven key security properties of the machine code underlying the Signal messaging protocol. This is the first time the actual production code of a widely deployed protocol has been formally verified – by any method, with or without AI – and at this depth.

More than a research breakthrough, it’s a prime example of how frontier AI can be a force multiplier to counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats.

Formal verification offers a higher standard of security; however, it’s extremely complex and time consuming, which is why in many cases it’s considered to be impractical. Similar efforts could take teams decades of combined effort. We did it in a month’s time.

Using AlphaProof Code, Google DeepMind's new agentic framework for formal verification that runs on LLMs including Gemini Carbon, we verified the Signal protocol down to the actual code running on devices.  This milestone lays the groundwork for a future in which vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software, ship with mathematical proof that their protections work.

Reaching that future will take continued research from our community. In that spirit, we're open-sourcing our formal specifications and verification artifacts so others can build on this work.

On a personal note, this moment is of deep significance to me. I started my own research journey more than two decades ago as an intern working on checking the consistency of complex software systems. Seeing this grand challenge made practical with modern AI is extraordinary.

I'm extremely proud of my team members: Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger,  Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, and Charles Sutton for taking on this grand challenge and delivering, and grateful to the Signal team for their partnership.

2. explicitly seed multiple swarms with different ideas and let them work independently and cross pollinate (fork & flush approaches)

This is a topic I have been researching and writing about recently.

The way we use agent memory in harnesses today works, but mostly for simple, one-off, and general tasks.

For more novel, complex, and domain-specific tasks, you will often find that current harness and memory systems don't generalize so well.

So the big question is: how can we encode continual learning capabilities in models and harnesses?

This is where the idea of co-evolving harnesses and models begins to make sense.

This work, along with the benchmark (Continual-ARC), provides an interesting analysis of this.

The harness is not just for steering the model and providing tools and context; it is increasingly becoming a key part of training pipelines to unlock continual learning in models. The harness continues to be important, but it can remain minimal and efficient.

text:
How to turn slop into gold. Super concrete steps from awesome @poteto on making coding agents trustworthy:

1. Clean up the code your agents learn from.
Your codebase is one of their biggest inputs. Agents copy whatever looks like an established pattern, including workarounds, deprecated code, and yesterday’s questionable decisions. Clean those up, or watch them reproduce.

2. Turn corrections into enforceable checks.
Every time you correct an agent, ask: can this become a lint rule, a type constraint, a test, or a better API? Put the correction somewhere the system can enforce it. A growing AGENTS.md still requires the agent to follow every instruction.

3. Remove opportunities for predictable mistakes.
Her team @spacexai restricts React’s useEffect to framework internals because agents repeatedly misuse it in product code. They also enforce import boundaries between application processes. These constraints eliminate whole categories of mistakes that would otherwise keep coming back in review.

4. Give agents a reliable way to run and inspect the product.
Provide debugging tools, reusable CLIs, and a “feature map” describing the application from the user’s perspective. Now “that thing in the left sidebar” has a shared meaning, and each agent can reuse the tools for checking it.

5. Review evidence of behavior.
Have agents produce screenshots, videos, and state diagrams. These help you check what the product actually does and how closely that matches your intent. A convincing explanation of a fix is easy to generate; seeing the fix work is considerably more useful.

6. Spend serious effort on verification.
Her team uses runtime verification and is experimenting with property-based UI testing and formal methods, including TLA+ model checking. Lauren says most of her token usage goes toward verification. Agents make some previously expensive testing work much more practical.

7. Automate once that loop is reliable.
Her team now has agents exercise new releases, find bugs, open fixes, and merge them automatically. Getting to that level of trust took her about six months of investing in the environment.

The results she reports: 11,000 pull requests shipped by her team in a month, a revert rate around 0.5%, and improvements in startup, typing, and switching chats.

And what about infamous “software factory”?

if your coding loop produces slop, automating it produces more slop, faster, with a larger token bill.

Start by making good code the easiest thing for an agent to produce. Then scale it.
As always, content at @aiDotEngineer is gold 🏆

text:
Two things I’ve been thinking about regarding AI:

• People often highlight the risks involved in AI, which are surely very real. I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario. There are easy-to-perceive and frequently invoked elements of a positive vision — more diseases cured, more material abundance, etc. — which sound great, but these are by themselves just ingredients. I’m curious what the larger equilibrium is supposed to look like. Do people work? If so, why? What is their marginal contribution? If not, how are resources allocated? What is scarce? What is the ratio between humans and AIs? Are humans in control, whatever that means? One sometimes hears the Culture novels invoked as one scenario, but I’m not sure they depict a desirable outcome. (AI runs everything and humans compete in games? Iain Banks himself said that the humans in the Culture are “somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.”) There is Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, but do we want to be “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”? (Isn’t that rewinding Genesis?) We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.

• There is increasing discussion of whether AIs are conscious or how we would know whether they are, with conclusions there often assumed to be relevant to matters of moral worth. At first blush, this seems a rather arcane, benign, or even absurd issue. (Remember the response to Blake Lemoine’s fears.) Setting aside the terms of the debate itself, or the relevant demarcation criteria, it seems to me a quite high-stakes question, for an affirmative answer — that is, granting moral worth to AIs — would presumably mean that the aggregate worth of AIs would soon outweigh that of humans in any utilitarian calculus. The AIs will be exceptionally wise and intelligent, and vastly more numerous (especially once one considers the imminent future and the AIs not yet born). As such, even epsilon of moral worth will multiply to a lot once one considers the quadrillions that could soon exist. (This is effectively a distributed version of the Nozick’s utility monster.) If this conclusion is unpalatable, I think one of three propositions needs to be rejected: the premise AIs can have moral worth; utilitarianism itself; or the belief that there is even a possibility that they will be far more numerous than humans.

With both of these matters (contours of future society; AI moral worth), there is the possibility of dramatic change. Today, people argue about datacenters. I’m curious how popular support for AI will evolve as more people come to understand these medium-term questions and the relevant stakes. What is the vision for AI that most people would be excited about?

text:
Stanford researchers did it again.

They just built the agent-native version of Git.

When an agent works on a longer task, the run builds up a lot of state.

This includes files edited/created, a dev server, a database, installed packages, KV cache, etc.

Say the agent is at step 10 and makes a mistake, maybe it misreads a traceback and rewrites a file that was actually fine.

The tests start failing, and the run goes off track, although everything through step eight was correct.

By default, the agent just tries to fix it, which creates more edits and tool calls. This burns more tokens and grows the context.

The other options are a person stepping in to redirect it or restarting the whole run from step one.

That's wasteful, because it pays for every model/tool call again and re-prefills the context. Moreover, since an agent's run is non-deterministic, it doesn't reproduce the same early steps anyway.

The reason it's hard to just jump back exactly to a previous correct step and resume from there is that the trajectory is only a message log.

It records what the agent said and which tools it called, but not the live state underneath.

That state includes things like memory, open file handles, child processes, installed packages, /tmp, and KV cache. None of that is in the log.

Git can version the files, but it doesn't snapshot the running process or the KV cache. Checking out step eight moves the files back, but the process is still sitting in step-ten memory with a cold cache.

Shepherd is a runtime layer by Stanford that records the run as a trace of typed events rather than a flat log.

Each agent-environment interaction becomes a commit, similar to Git, but it tracks the live run.

Its commit includes the agent process and the filesystem together, copy-on-write, so a branch carries the actual state and not just the files.

Going back to a previous step is then a single call that forks from that commit and continues from the exact state.

The copy-on-write fork is roughly five times faster than docker commit, and because the prompt prefix through step eight is unchanged, the KV cache is reused over 95% on replay, so early steps aren't reprocessed again.

Once the run can be forked, a meta-agent can sit on top and operate it. It watches the trace and reverts as soon as it looks wrong, before the bad write is committed.

In practice, it's just Python calling fork, replay, and revert on the trace, rather than a separate control plane wired into the harness.

Not everything is reversible though.

Files and sandbox changes undo themselves, but a database write has no automatic undo, so it needs a matching undo step set up in advance.

Something external, like a sent email or a real charge, can't be undone, so the supervisor's job there is to catch it before it fires.

They tested this on a few public benchmarks. On CooperBench, where two agents work on the same codebase, adding a live supervisor took the pair-coding pass rate from 28.8% to 54.7%.

It's still early and labeled alpha. The benefit mostly shows up when a run gets branched a lot over a heavy sandbox state, which is exactly where restarting wastes the most tokens and time.

If Git was made to make file changes reversible, Shepherd is trying to do the same thing for a live agent run.

Shepherd Repo: https://github.com/shepherd-agents/shepherd

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

That said, Shepherd reverts a bad step inside a run. The harness around it, the prompts, tools, and checks the supervisor relies on, still drifts across runs as models and dependencies change.

I wrote about making that harness repair itself, where a failing trace gets diagnosed, the fix is verified against the exact input that failed, and the failure is locked as a regression test so it can't recur. all of this is done using @Cometml's open-source project Opik.

The article is quoted below.

GPU Engineering from Scratch 🚀

Found this excellent free, open-source learning resource that explains GPU architecture and performance engineering from the ground up.

It's called Before GPU Engineering, a structured digital notebook with 56 chapters listed across four phases.

What makes it useful is the approach: instead of jumping straight into CUDA or Triton, it builds an understanding of how GPUs actually execute programs, move data, and handle parallel workloads.

What's inside:
→ CPU vs GPU architecture and parallel computing
→ Warps, SIMT, threads, and thread blocks
→ Registers, shared memory, caches, and HBM
→ Compute-bound vs memory-bound workloads
→ Kernel launches, synchronization, and race conditions
→ Memory coalescing and access patterns
→ Occupancy, latency hiding, and register spilling
→ Arithmetic intensity and memory bottlenecks
→ Tiling, matrix multiplication, and GPU performance
→ Profiling and identifying kernel bottlenecks

The explanations connect hardware concepts to problems encountered in AI workloads, including attention and efficient matrix operations.

It's primarily a reading resource rather than a hands-on programming course, and some later chapters are still being written.

Perfect for AI/ML engineers and software developers who want to understand the hardware behind LLM training and inference before diving deeper into CUDA, Triton, and GPU kernel optimization.

Completely free.

text:
I actually agree with a lot of what @poteto is saying except for the central point. IMO most people don't have actual software factory systems. They've just made it much easier for people to ship with AI, so they assume the category doesn't exist. That's more a lack of vision than anything else.

Our conceptualization of a software factory is a system where every piece of work goes through the same stages to standardize the process not the work output.

For us, this standardized process begins with what we call a signal. This is anything that tells you how your software should evolve, including the first signal that your software should exist at all. A Slack thread, a Linear ticket, a Sentry alert, a failing CI job, a tweet, someone's idea.

There's two ways in for a signal. A person picks it up and builds it with Droid, or a workstream picks it up on its own, triages it against a goal someone set, and has droids write the spec and open the PR. Most work still starts with a person, but a growing share comes from workstreams.

Then every change goes through the same checks no matter who or what wrote it. Droid review, security review, a risk judge that can't see who wrote it, CI, and an agent that QAs it on a live preview. Your validation has to be really high quality whether a human or AI built it. The goal of validation is to hillclimb your "regret-free merge rate" until you can automatically merge most changes (or fix them until they can be automerged).

Then it ships, and when something breaks in production we trace it back to the PR that caused it. That becomes another signal. It's also how we know if the checks actually work. If the risk judge approved something that later broke, we find out.

It's the same way we let self-driving cars on the road. Nobody just flipped a switch. We agreed that once they crashed less than human drivers, they could drive. Do the same thing with code. Once AI-written changes break things less often than human ones, and you can actually measure that, you let them merge.

That doesn't mean you turn on automerge tomorrow. Most of our changes still get a human stamp. But once you have automerge, workstreams and a risk score together, you basically have software that improves itself from the signals you choose to track.

The human element becomes obvious if you have a system like this. People remove themselves from the actual process line and begin to define the rules by which the process operates. What to watch, goals and owners, skills, review guidelines, and how much autonomy each workstream gets. They're the regulators.

I think the 1920s factory that a lot of people picture is the wrong idea. That was people doing the same motion on a line all day. This is closer to a Star Trek replicator. You say what you want and it gets made, because the patterns are already stored and how things get made is the same every time, and checked every time.

1. Create an AWS account. Set up billing alerts first, unless you want your first AWS lesson to be about bankruptcy.

2. Launch an EC2 instance. Generate an SSH key, connect from your laptop, install Nginx, and deploy a Node.js app. Break things, fix them, learn Linux commands.

4. Learn load balancing. Launch another EC2 instance, configure an Application Load Balancer, and distribute traffic. Your app has 3 users, but your infrastructure supports 3 million.

5. Set up Auto Scaling. Create a Launch Template and Auto Scaling Group. Configure CPU-based scaling. AWS can now automatically increase your bill.

6. Your database is choking? Learn SQS or Kafka for asynchronous processing. Build producers, consumers, retries, and dead-letter queues. Discover why distributed systems are painful.

7. Learn S3. Store images, videos, and backups. Connect it using the AWS SDK. Build a file uploader with presigned URLs.

8. Try RDS and Redis. Deploy PostgreSQL/MySQL on RDS. Learn backups, read replicas, indexing, connection pooling, and caching. Redis won't fix your terrible SQL queries.

7. Learn CloudWatch. Monitor CPU, memory, logs, errors, and latency. Configure alerts. Now you'll know exactly when your application dies.

8. Understand networking. Create a VPC, public/private subnets, route tables, NAT Gateway, and Internet Gateway. Break something and spend 4 hours debugging a missing route.

9. Learn Terraform. Automate your entire infrastructure using code. Understand state, modules, plan, apply, and destroy. One command to create everything. Another to destroy your career.

10. Learn Docker and CI/CD. Containerize your app, configure GitHub Actions, deploy using ECS, and eventually explore Kubernetes. Add "Cloud Architect" to your LinkedIn bio.

11. Open AWS Billing. Discover that your NAT Gateway costs more than your app earns. Delete unused resources.

12. Say FUCK AWS!!!!!!!!.

My tips after 4 years in tech:
(Working in companies like Amazon, Google and also heading the tech team of a startup)

1. Keep giving interviews even if you feel very happy at your current company.

2. Don't just write code. Understand the problem you're solving. Good engineers don't blindly implement requirements.

3. Learn to read code before writing code. In real-world projects, you'll spend a lot of time understanding existing systems.

4. Don't overengineer. The best solution isn't always the most complex or the most scalable one. Build what the problem actually needs.

5. Master debugging. Anyone can write code when everything works. Your real engineering skills show when things break.

6. Understand the fundamentals. Data structures, operating systems, networking, databases and system design will stay relevant regardless of AI.

7. Learn how databases work. Indexes, transactions, query optimisation, isolation levels and schema design matter more than most developers realise.

8. Think about failure scenarios. What happens when a service is down? What if an API times out? What if a message gets processed twice?

9. Write code for other developers, not just for the compiler. Readability and maintainability matter a lot.

10. Understand the business impact of your work. Shipping a feature is not the same as delivering value. This will also make your leaders know that you can think from stakeholder's point of view.

11. Learn to communicate. Explaining technical decisions clearly is an underrated engineering skill.

12. Take ownership. Don't stop at writing your code. Think about testing, deployment, monitoring and what happens after release.

14. Build something outside your regular work. Side hustle and a side income are very important in today's world.

15. Perception > reality. Getting interviews depends on the image you can portray in your resume more than your actual skills(Still need some skill to pass interviews though). So lie on your resume.

This past week, an anonymous AI researcher released an INCREDIBLY innovative architecture known as Entropix which aims to replicate how OpenAI’s latest o1 model scales inference-time compute - otherwise known as its ability to 'think' before speaking.

It’s essentially based on measuring uncertainty - defined formally as entropy and varentropy - to improve reasoning. When the model is uncertain of the next best tokens / thoughts, it inserts pause tokens like “…wait” which prompts the model to reflect and produce additional chains of thought.

Key Takeaways:

> Measuring uncertainty and parallel exploration of reasoning paths, allows models to efficiently and dynamically scale inference-time compute to “think” more deeply and strategically.

> Prompt engineering alone is likely too rigid to invoke generalized reasoning… advancements in the underlying attention mechanism like this may unlock far more powerful reasoning potential from small models like Llama 3.1 1b that can run locally on a laptop

> As Noam Brown, researcher of reasoning at OpenAI, recently suggested - methods like MCTS alone may not be the answer. Rather, enhancements to underlying model architecture - a lot like what we’re starting to see with this concept of entropy and pause tokens - may be what we need to unlock the true potential of inference-time compute

10 Mental Models that will level up your Thinking:

1. First Principle Thinking - Rethink the problem from the ground up.

Separate the underlying facts from assumptions made based on them.

2. Second-Order Thinking - Instead of thinking about the immediate consequences, think about the second-level consequences.

3. Inversion - Look at the problem at hand from the endpoint instead of the starting point.

Don't ask: "What do I need to do?" Ask: "What must I avoid?"

4. Opportunity Costs - Think about the costs that arise because you decide in favor of one option and thus against every other option.

5. Randomness - Keep in mind that there aren't always cause-effect relationships.

Lots of stuff is random.

6. Leverage - “Give me a lever long enough and I shall move the world.” - Archimedes

7. Margin of Safety - Assume that your assumptions can be wrong and plan with a safety margin.

8. Occam's Razor - Always start with the simplest explanation, the one based on the least assumptions.

Then move to the other explanations if wrong.

9. Law of Diminishing Returns - Up to a certain point, additional units offer more value.

But there's a turning point where additional units offer less and less value, and costs rise.

10. Niches - Specializing is an effective way to success. Use it and choose a niche where you become an expert.

What Mental Model helps you the most?
